title: White Dot Syndromes: Masterclass in Posterior Uveitis
summary: A complex spectrum of idiopathic inflammatory chorioretinopathies affecting the outer retina, RPE, and choroid. This guide provides a residency-level deep dive into diagnosis, multimodal imaging, and evidence-based management of 'The White Dots'.

sections.title: The Big Five: Clinical Presentation
content: Acute onset photopsia (hallmark of MEWDS and AZOOR)
Painless blurred vision (unilateral vs. bilateral)
Central or paracentral scotomata
Nyctalopia (prominent in Birdshot and AZOOR)
Dyschromatopsia (correlating with outer retinal damage)

rows: Hyper-AF dots (more than visible on fundus)

sections.title: The Pathognomonic 'Foveal Granularity'
sections.content: Specific to MEWDS (Multiple Evanescent White Dot Syndrome), this appears as fine orange-yellow granular changes in the fovea. On OCT, this corresponds to disruption of the Ellipsoid Zone (EZ) and accumulation of hyperreflective material at the RPE/Photoreceptor interface. It typically resolves completely without treatment.

sections.title: Diagnostic Workflow (The WDS Workup)
content: Step 1: Rule out Infection (FTA-ABS, RPR, QuantiFERON-TB Gold, CXR).
Step 2: Baseline Multimodal Imaging (FAF, OCT, FFA, ICG).
Step 3: HLA-A29 testing if Birdshot suspected.
Step 4: ERG (30Hz Flicker) for functional monitoring in Birdshot/AZOOR.
Step 5: Neurological review if APMPPE present (Stroke/Vasculitis risk).

sections.title: Birdshot Chorioretinopathy: Deep Dive
content: Strongest HLA association in medicine: HLA-A29 (>95%).
Classic 'Creamy' lesions radiating from the optic nerve in the inferior/nasal quadrant.
Commonly presents with Vitritis and Cystoid Macular Edema (CME).
Standard of Care: Long-term IMT (Mycophenolate Mofetil or Cyclosporine) to avoid steroid side effects.
Monitoring: Gold standard is the Electroretinogram (ERG) - look for 30Hz flicker delay and b-wave amplitude decrease.

sections.title: Red Flags: When to Worry
content: Sudden drop in vision with subretinal hemorrhage (CNVM).
CNS symptoms in APMPPE (Cerebral Vasculitis).
Persistent vitritis in an older patient (Lymphoma).
Positive Syphilis serology (Penicillin G required immediately).

content.explanation: P: Posterior, L: Late staining on FA, A: Acute onset, C: CNS involvement risk, O: Outer retinal/RPE level, I: ICG hypofluorescence, D: Decidedly bilateral (usually).

sections.title: Management & Treatment Protocols
content: 1. Observation: Indicated for MEWDS and simple APMPPE (often self-limiting).
2. Systemic Corticosteroids: 1mg/kg Prednisone for active Serpiginous or Birdshot flares.
3. Immunomodulatory Therapy (IMT): Required for Serpiginous, Birdshot, and chronic MFC/PIC (Steroid sparing).
4. Anti-VEGF: Intravitreal injections (Ranibizumab/Aflibercept) for inflammatory CNVM.
5. Laser/PDT: Rarely used, generally avoided in active inflammatory lesions.

sections.title: AZOOR: The Occult Threat
content: Normal fundus initially, hence 'Occult'.
Marked Photopsia and field loss.
FAF: Shows a distinct 'tri-zonal' progression of RPE loss.
OCT: Abrupt loss of the EZ line at the border of the scotoma.
Treatment is controversial; often involves systemic immunosuppression.

sections.title: Landmark Studies & Updates
content: Gass (1968): Original description of APMPPE.
Jampol (1984): Original description of MEWDS.
OCT-Angiography (OCT-A): Modern studies show choriocapillaris flow voids in APMPPE and Serpiginous, suggesting a primary vasculopathy.
MUST Trial: High-yield reference for systemic vs. local steroid delivery in uveitis management.

sections.title: Clinical Pearl: The MEWDS 'Enigma'
sections.content: MEWDS is frequently misdiagnosed as Optic Neuritis due to the presence of an afferent pupillary defect (APD) and disc edema. Always check the fovea for granularity and perform FAF/ICG to reveal the characteristic dots that clinch the diagnosis and spare the patient a costly and unnecessary neurologic workup.
